title: Organising labour

blocks.heading: Organising labour
blocks.text: Labour contributes physical and mental effort; dividing tasks can allow workers to specialise. Repeated practice and less switching between suitable tasks can improve output, but poor coordination or repetitive work may limit the gains. In a bag-making group, separate cutting, stitching and finishing roles can let workers build skill in a task. Work must pass between stages at a workable pace. If cutting outruns stitching, unfinished pieces accumulate instead of completed bags. Explain the connection between organisation and useful output rather than assuming any division makes workers faster.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Division of labour
blocks.text: Division of labour is splitting production into specialised tasks carried out by different workers. Dividing tasks describes the arrangement of work, whereas mass production describes producing large quantities of standardised output. Three workers can divide cutting, stitching and checking even in a small workshop. A large output figure alone does not show who performs each task. The separating test is whether the description states a task allocation or merely a quantity. A process may use both division of labour and mass production.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Specialisation
blocks.text: Specialisation is concentrating on a narrower range of tasks or products to develop skills or efficiency. Specialised work may improve proficiency but can create dependence on others for the remaining tasks or products. A worker specialising in stitching can gain speed through practice, while depending on others to cut pieces accurately. A producer may specialise in one crop or service rather than one factory task. The term is therefore broader than a specific division of labour inside a workshop.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Coordinate tasks rather than count workers
blocks.text: Three workers in an invented workshop each make a complete bag, repeatedly switching tools. They could divide cutting, stitching and checking if each learns the task and pieces move between stages reliably. Practice and fewer changes may improve useful output. If stitching is slower, assigning more cutting will merely increase the queue. A suitable task allocation addresses the bottleneck. The number of bags produced does not reveal whether tasks were divided, which separates division of labour from mass production.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect production to development
blocks.text: Technology changes which tasks people perform. Link the organisation of labour to the flow of useful output and keep task division distinct from the quantity produced.
